sentences.text: Vinialesaurus possessed a long, thin neck that ended in a relatively small head.
Its body was rounded and it had a medium-length tail.
The animal had serrated teeth, indicating it was a carnivore.
Estimates suggest the animal measured between four and ten meters in length and weighed between one and three tons.
It possessed paddle-like flippers adapted for swimming in warm waters.
It coexisted with the bivalve Trigonia krombelli, a genus that still exists in Australia.
The species was first described in 1949 as a subspecies of Cryptocleidus by Ricardo De la Torre and Luis Rojas.
The genus was redescribed and elevated to a distinct genus in 2002 by Zulma Gasparini, Bardet, and Iturralde.
The genus name honors the town of Viñales in western Cuba where the fossils were found.
The species name honors the original discoverer, Carlos de la Torre y Huerta.
The holotype fossil was prepared at the American Museum of Natural History between 1991 and 1992.
A second specimen was discovered in the Atacama Desert, specifically in Calama, Chile.
Placoderms, which were abundant in the Oxfordian, likely constituted part of its diet.
Other marine reptiles may have been the main competitors of Vinialesaurus.
The pliosaur Peloneustes was a predator with massive jaws nearly one meter long.
Taxonomically, Vinialesaurus belongs to the family Cryptoclididae.
This plesiosaur lived during the Late Jurassic (Oxfordian) in the Jagua Formation of Pinar del Río, Cuba.
The animal lived approximately 150 million years ago.
It lived in a diverse ecosystem located in the proto-Caribbean.
The Proto-Caribbean developed in a channel created between the continents of Laurasia and Gondwana.
Turtles such as Caribemys oxfordiensis likely nested in the same environment.
The time range for this genus is the Oxfordian stage, from 159 to 154.8 million years ago.
